entry: Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series by Hirohiko Araki. It was serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* from 1987 to 2004 and then in *Ultra Jump*. Its nine story arcs each feature a new protagonist bearing the JoJo nickname. Battles center on Stands, psycho-spiritual manifestations of a person's fighting spirit. The series is known for its art style, character poses and references to Western popular music and [[Fashion]]. Over 120 million copies were in circulation by August 2023, and the franchise includes anime, a live-action film and video games.

American folk singer and activist. She began recording in 1960 and has released more than 30 albums; although a songwriter herself, she generally interprets others' songs. She was one of the first major artists to record songs by [[Bob Dylan]] and did much to popularize his early work. Her activism has focused on nonviolence, civil rights, human rights and the environment. She performed at the 1969 [[Woodstock|Woodstock Festival]] and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2017.

English actress, author and columnist. Collins starred as Alexis Colby in the soap opera *Dynasty* from 1981 to 1989, a role that made her an international star and won her a Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Television Series – Drama in 1982. Her films include *Land of the Pharaohs* (1955), made during her contract with 20th Century Fox. Her later television roles include *The Royals* and *American Horror Story: Apocalypse*. In 2015 Queen [[Elizabeth II]] made her a Dame for her charitable work, particularly on behalf of children.

American actress. Signed by [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] in 1925, Crawford became one of Hollywood's most prominent stars, often playing hardworking young women who find romance and financial success. By the end of the 1930s her films were losing money, and she was labeled "box office poison." Her comeback in *Mildred Pierce* (1945) won her the Academy Award for Best Actress. After marrying Alfred Steele, president of [[Pepsi|Pepsi-Cola]], she was elected to the company's board after his death in 1959. She retired from the screen after *Trog* (1970). After her death, her daughter Christina published the memoir *Mommie Dearest*.

American writer and journalist. One of the pioneers of New Journalism, Didion began her career in the 1950s after winning an essay contest sponsored by [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]. Her novel *Play It as It Lays* (1970) is considered a classic of American fiction. In 1991 she wrote the earliest mainstream media article to suggest that the Central Park Five had been wrongfully convicted. Her memoir *The Year of Magical Thinking* (2005), about the year after her husband's sudden death, won the National Book Award for Nonfiction. In 2013 [[Barack Obama|President Barack Obama]] awarded her the National Humanities Medal.

American rock singer, songwriter and guitarist. Jett co-founded the Runaways in 1975 and performed with them until their breakup in 1979. After several labels rejected her first solo album, she founded the independent Blackheart Records and formed Joan Jett and the Blackhearts. Their cover of "I Love Rock 'n Roll" from the album *I Love Rock 'n Roll* (1981) topped the U.S. Billboard Hot 100. In 2015 she and the Blackhearts were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. [[Rolling Stone]] included her on its lists of the greatest guitarists, and she starred with [[Michael J. Fox]] in *Light of Day* (1987).

Catalan painter, sculptor and ceramicist. Miró was born in [[Barcelona]] and moved to [[Paris]] in 1920, though he spent his summers in Catalonia. His early work was influenced by [[Vincent van Gogh]] and [[Paul Cézanne]]. He joined the [[Surrealism|Surrealist]] group in 1924, but his personal style resists easy classification and often reflects Catalan pride. In interviews from the 1930s onward, he expressed contempt for conventional painting, which he called an "assassination of painting." His output includes [[Mural|murals]], among them works for [[UNESCO]]. The Fundació Joan Miró opened in Barcelona in 1975, and a second museum opened in 1981 in his adoptive city of [[Mallorca|Palma, Mallorca]].

American comedian and television host. Rivers began in comedy clubs in Greenwich Village alongside [[George Carlin]], [[Woody Allen]] and [[Richard Pryor]]. Her blunt, self-deprecating and often controversial humor targeted celebrities and politicians. Her 1965 guest appearances on *The Tonight Show*, hosted by her mentor [[Johnny Carson]], established her style. In 1986 she became the first woman to host a late-night network [[Talk show|talk show]], *The Late Show with Joan Rivers*. She later co-hosted E!'s *Fashion Police* and won a Daytime Emmy for *The Joan Rivers Show*. She authored 12 best-selling books.

Australian dramatic coloratura soprano. Sutherland contributed to the revival of the [[Opera|bel canto]] repertoire from the late 1950s to the 1980s. Born in [[Sydney]], she made her debut at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, in 1952. Her voice combined agility, accurate intonation, pinpoint staccatos, a trill and a strong upper register, although critics complained about her diction. In 1959 she sang Lucia in Donizetti's *Lucia di Lammermoor* at Covent Garden, and she sang the role to acclaim in Paris in 1960 and at La Scala and the Metropolitan Opera in 1961. Her husband, conductor Richard Bonynge, encouraged her to focus on bel canto roles. She was the first Australian to win a Grammy Award, for the 1961 Best Classical Performance – Vocal Soloist, presented in 1962. Known as La Stupenda, she was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1979.

French folk heroine and patron saint of France. Born into a propertied peasant family at Domrémy, she said she was guided by visions from the [[Michael (archangel)|archangel Michael]], Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine to help Charles VII save France from English domination. She arrived at Orléans with a relief army in April 1429, and the English abandoned the siege nine days later. Her campaigns opened the way for Charles to be crowned at Reims during the [[Hundred Years' War]]. Captured by Burgundian troops in 1430, she was handed to the English, tried for heresy and burned at the stake at about age 19. A retrial in 1456 overturned the verdict. Joan was canonized in 1920 and, two years later, declared one of the patron saints of France. She is popularly revered as a martyr.

American actress. Woodward won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *The Three Faces of Eve* (1957), playing a woman with [[Dissociative identity disorder|dissociative identity disorder]]. She was married to [[Paul Newman]] for 50 years, until his death, and the two often worked together. Her mother named her after [[Joan Crawford]]. Woodward has won three Primetime Emmy Awards, a British Academy Film Award and three Golden Globe Awards. In 1990 she earned a bachelor's degree from Sarah Lawrence College at age 60, graduating alongside her daughter Clea. She is the oldest living Best Actress Oscar winner.

American actor. Credited as Leaf Phoenix early in his career, he gained critical acclaim for supporting roles in *To Die For* (1995) and *Quills* (2000). He was nominated for an Academy Award for playing [[Commodus]] in *Gladiator* (2000), and he won a Grammy Award and a Golden Globe for his portrayal of [[Johnny Cash]] in *Walk the Line* (2005). He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for the title role in *Joker* (2019). Phoenix is also a vegan [[Animal rights|animal rights]] activist who has produced documentaries on global meat consumption.

Mongol prince and military commander. Jochi was the son of Börte, wife of Temüjin, later known as [[Genghis Khan]]. Because Börte had been held captive by the Merkit tribe, his paternity was doubted, and his brother Chagatai and others viewed him as illegitimate. Temüjin nevertheless regarded Jochi as his son, and after founding the [[Mongol Empire]] in 1206 he entrusted him with a large territory in the west. Jochi led campaigns to extend Mongol power there and was a prominent commander in the invasion of the [[Khwarazmian Empire]] (1219–1221). Tensions with his family, particularly over the 1221 siege of Gurganj, never healed. He was still estranged when he died. His son Batu was appointed to rule his territories, and Jochi's descendants ruled the [[Golden Horde]].

City (pop., 2025: 1.6 million) in [[Rajasthan]], northwestern India. Jodhpur, the second-largest city in the state after [[Jaipur]], is the historic capital of the Kingdom of Marwar. Rao Jodha, a Rajput chief of the Rathore clan, founded it in 1459. It is the administrative headquarters of Jodhpur district. On August 11, 1947, its last ruler, Maharaja Hanwant Singh, signed the Instrument of Accession, merging the state into the Union of India. Situated in the Thar Desert, the city has a [[Desert climate|hot desert climate]], and temperatures routinely exceed 40 °C from April to June. The highest temperature recorded was 48.8 °C on May 20, 2016. The old town, which circles the Mehrangarh Fort, is known as the Blue City for the dominant blue of its buildings. Jodhpur is a major tourist destination known for its forts, palaces and temples.

American actress and filmmaker. A child model and Disney teen idol, Foster was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing a 12-year-old prostitute in [[Martin Scorsese]]'s [[Taxi Driver]] (1976). After attending [[Yale University]], she won two Academy Awards for Best Actress, for *The Accused* (1988) and *The Silence of the Lambs* (1991). She has directed four feature films, including *Little Man Tate* (1991) and *Money Monster* (2016). On [[HBO]] she starred in *True Detective: Night Country* (2024), which won her a Primetime Emmy Award and a Golden Globe.

American politician and 46th president of the United States (2021–2025). A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he represented Delaware in the [[United States Senate]] from 1973 to 2009 and was vice president under [[Barack Obama]] from 2009 to 2017. As president he signed the American Rescue Plan Act in response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and imposed sanctions on [[Russia]] after its invasion of [[Ukraine]]. U.S. troops left Afghanistan during his presidency, ending the war there. After his performance in the first presidential debate of 2024, he withdrew his candidacy for reelection. He is the oldest person to have served as president.

American baseball center fielder. Born to Italian immigrants in California, DiMaggio played his entire 13-year career with the [[New York Yankees]] in [[Major League Baseball]]. He set the record for the longest hitting streak, 56 games from May 15 to July 16, 1941. A three-time American League Most Valuable Player, he played on Yankees teams that won nine World Series championships during his tenure. He was inducted into the [[Baseball|Baseball Hall of Fame]] in 1955 and was voted the sport's greatest living player in a 1969 poll. He is also widely known for his marriage to [[Marilyn Monroe]] and his lifelong devotion to her.

American heavyweight boxer. Nicknamed Smokin' Joe, Frazier won a gold medal at the 1964 Summer Olympics and was undisputed heavyweight champion from 1970 to 1973. Known for relentless pressure, he defeated [[Muhammad Ali]] by unanimous decision in the 1971 Fight of the Century. He lost his title to [[George Foreman]] in 1973 and was beaten by Ali again in the 1975 Thrilla in Manila. Frazier retired in 1976 after a second loss to Foreman, returned for one fight in 1981 and finished with a record of 32 wins, four losses and one draw. He later trained fighters at his gym in [[Philadelphia]].

American professional boxer. Nicknamed the Brown Bomber, he is considered one of the greatest boxers in history. He was world heavyweight champion from 1937 until his retirement in 1949 and made 25 consecutive title defenses, a record for all weight classes. Born in rural Alabama, he moved with his family to [[Detroit]], Michigan, in 1926. He had three losses in 69 professional fights. His 1938 rematch victory over German boxer Max Schmeling made him a focal point of anti-Nazi sentiment before and during [[World War II]]. He is regarded as the first Black American to become a nationwide hero in the United States.

American football quarterback. Montana played 16 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), mostly with the [[San Francisco]] 49ers. He won four [[Super Bowl|Super Bowls]] with San Francisco and was named Super Bowl Most Valuable Player three times. Nicknamed Joe Cool, he was named NFL Most Valuable Player in 1989 and 1990. His game-winning touchdown pass to Dwight Clark against [[Dallas]] in the 1981 NFC Championship Game, known as the Catch, is a staple of NFL highlight films. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2000 and later became a venture capitalist.

American actor and musician. Pesci is best known for tough, volatile characters in a variety of genres and for his films with [[Martin Scorsese]] and [[Robert De Niro]]. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *Goodfellas* (1990) and received two further nominations in the category, for *Raging Bull* (1980) and *The Irishman* (2019). He is also known for comic roles in *Home Alone* (1990) and the *Lethal Weapon* films. Born in [[Newark, New Jersey]], he retired from acting in 1999 but has returned periodically. He has also recorded three studio albums.

American podcaster and sports commentator. Rogan began comedy in [[Boston]] in 1988 and hosted *Fear Factor* from 2001 to 2006. Since 1997 he has worked as a commentator for the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship]]. His podcast, *The Joe Rogan Experience*, became one of the most popular in the world. A 2020 deal with [[Spotify]] was valued at $200 million; a 2024 renewal, estimated at $250 million, ended its exclusivity. Critics accuse him of promoting conspiracy theories and [[COVID-19]] misinformation; he has supported [[Same-sex marriage|same-sex marriage]], gun rights and free speech. He endorsed [[Donald Trump]] in the 2024 presidential election, though he later criticized some Trump policies.

Dutch footballer and manager. Regarded as one of the greatest players in history, Cruyff won the Ballon d'Or three times, in 1971, 1973 and 1974. He was a leading proponent of Total Football, the style developed by Rinus Michels. At Ajax he won six [[Eredivisie]] titles, three European Cups and an Intercontinental Cup. In 1973 he moved to [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]], winning the club's first [[La Liga]] title in 14 years in 1973–74. He led the Netherlands to the 1974 [[FIFA World Cup]] final, where they lost to West Germany, and received the Golden Ball. He refused to play in the 1978 World Cup after a kidnapping attempt against him and his family, ending his international career. As Barcelona's manager he won four La Liga titles and one European Cup. In 1999 he was voted European Player of the Century, second behind [[Pelé]] in the World Player of the Century poll.

Swiss mathematician and member of the prominent Bernoulli family. Known for his contributions to [[Calculus|infinitesimal calculus]], Johann Bernoulli also taught [[Leonhard Euler]] as a young man. Born in [[Basel]], he studied medicine at its university and mathematics with his older brother [[Jacob Bernoulli]]; together they were among the first to apply calculus to problems. He defended [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] in the Leibniz–Newton dispute over credit for calculus, showing that Leibniz's methods solved problems that [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] had not. He held the mathematics chair at Groningen before succeeding his brother at Basel. A rivalry with his son Daniel led him to deliberately and falsely predate his *Hydraulica* by six years.

German philosopher. A founding figure of German idealism, which developed from the writings of [[Immanuel Kant]], Fichte was motivated, like Descartes and Kant, by the problem of subjectivity and [[Consciousness|consciousness]]. He originated the thesis–antithesis–synthesis scheme, an idea often wrongly attributed to Hegel. He taught philosophy at Jena until 1799, when he was dismissed amid the "atheism controversy" over one of his essays. He later lectured in Berlin, where he wrote on [[Political philosophy|political philosophy]] and is regarded as one of the fathers of German nationalism. His *Addresses to the German Nation* (1807–1808), delivered during the [[Napoleon|Napoleonic]] occupation of Prussia, called for educational reform and national unity. Critics charge that the lectures fostered ethnic exclusivity, while others stress their emphasis on voluntary ethical commitment.
